claim: Circulating levels of AnxA1 were reduced in dengue patients compared to healthy controls.
source: Interestingly, we have identified that plasma levels of AnxA1 were reduced in dengue patients compared to healthy controls (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of AnxA1 in plasma samples from dengue patients (n=60) and healthy controls (n=41), shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Severe dengue patients had significantly lower levels of AnxA1 compared to individuals with classic dengue.
source: Stratification of groups according to disease severity at discharge showed that SD patients had discrete but significantly lower levels of AnxA1 compared to individuals with classic dengue (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements comparing AnxA1 levels between non-severe dengue (n=31) and severe dengue (n=29) patients, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DENV infection causes a time-dependent decline in plasma AnxA1 concentration in BALB/c mice.
source: In both DENV-infected BALB/c (Figure 1B) and C57BL/6 mice (Figure 1C), there was a time-dependent decline in the concentration of plasma AnxA1 compared to mock-infected animals.
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of plasma AnxA1 at multiple time points (24, 48, 72, 96 hours) after DENV-2 infection in BALB/c mice (n=8), shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DENV infection causes a time-dependent decline in plasma AnxA1 concentration in C57BL/6 mice.
source: In both DENV-infected BALB/c (Figure 1B) and C57BL/6 mice (Figure 1C), there was a time-dependent decline in the concentration of plasma AnxA1 compared to mock-infected animals.
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of plasma AnxA1 at multiple time points after DENV-2 infection in C57BL/6 mice (n=5-6), shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AnxA1 plasma levels in humans are higher than in animal samples.
source: Curiously, AnxA1 levels in human plasma were higher than in animal samples.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of AnxA1 ELISA measurements between human (Figure 1A) and mouse (Figure 1B-C) plasma samples.

claim: Differences in AnxA1 plasma levels between humans and mice have been previously noted.
source: Differences in AnxA1 plasma levels between both species have been previously noted (Senchenkova et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications documenting species differences in AnxA1 levels.

claim: AnxA1 KO animals showed more severe and prolonged thrombocytopenia than WT mice after DENV infection.
source: In the absence of AnxA1, animals showed more severe and prolonged thrombocytopenia, haemoconcentration, and vascular permeability than WT mice (Figure 2B–D), indicating a protective role of AnxA1 in dengue disease.
evidence: Supported by platelet count measurements in AnxA1 KO vs WT BALB/c mice after DENV-2 infection (n=6-8), shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AnxA1 KO animals showed more severe and prolonged haemoconcentration than WT mice after DENV infection.
source: In the absence of AnxA1, animals showed more severe and prolonged thrombocytopenia, haemoconcentration, and vascular permeability than WT mice (Figure 2B–D), indicating a protective role of AnxA1 in dengue disease.
evidence: Supported by haematocrit measurements in AnxA1 KO vs WT BALB/c mice after DENV-2 infection (n=6-8), shown in Figure 2C.

claim: AnxA1 KO animals showed more severe and prolonged vascular permeability than WT mice after DENV infection.
source: In the absence of AnxA1, animals showed more severe and prolonged thrombocytopenia, haemoconcentration, and vascular permeability than WT mice (Figure 2B–D), indicating a protective role of AnxA1 in dengue disease.
evidence: Supported by Evans blue vascular leakage assay in AnxA1 KO vs WT BALB/c mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 2D.

claim: AnxA1 plays a protective role in dengue disease.
source: In the absence of AnxA1, animals showed more severe and prolonged thrombocytopenia, haemoconcentration, and vascular permeability than WT mice (Figure 2B–D), indicating a protective role of AnxA1 in dengue disease.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AnxA1 KO mice show worse disease parameters than WT mice after DENV infection.

claim: FPR2 KO animals showed disease parameters similar to AnxA1 KO animals after DENV infection.
source: These findings were similar in FPR2-depleted animals (Figure 2G–I), suggesting that these effects are due to disruption of the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway.
evidence: Supported by measurements of thrombocytopenia, haemoconcentration, and vascular permeability in FPR2 KO vs WT C57BL/6 mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: The protective effects of AnxA1 in dengue are due to the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway.
source: These findings were similar in FPR2-depleted animals (Figure 2G–I), suggesting that these effects are due to disruption of the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity of disease phenotypes between AnxA1 KO and FPR2 KO mice after DENV infection.

claim: Plasma levels of MCPT-1 were increased in AnxA1 KO animals compared to WT controls after DENV infection.
source: Plasma levels of mast cell protease 1 (MCPT-1) and CCL2 were increased in either AnxA1 and FPR2 KO animals compared to their respective controls after infection (Figure 2E, F, J and K).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of MCPT-1 in plasma from AnxA1 KO vs WT BALB/c mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Plasma levels of CCL2 were increased in AnxA1 KO animals compared to WT controls after DENV infection.
source: Plasma levels of mast cell protease 1 (MCPT-1) and CCL2 were increased in either AnxA1 and FPR2 KO animals compared to their respective controls after infection (Figure 2E, F, J and K).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of CCL2 in plasma from AnxA1 KO vs WT BALB/c mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Plasma levels of MCPT-1 were increased in FPR2 KO animals compared to WT controls after DENV infection.
source: Plasma levels of mast cell protease 1 (MCPT-1) and CCL2 were increased in either AnxA1 and FPR2 KO animals compared to their respective controls after infection (Figure 2E, F, J and K).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of MCPT-1 in plasma from FPR2 KO vs WT C57BL/6 mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Plasma levels of CCL2 were increased in FPR2 KO animals compared to WT controls after DENV infection.
source: Plasma levels of mast cell protease 1 (MCPT-1) and CCL2 were increased in either AnxA1 and FPR2 KO animals compared to their respective controls after infection (Figure 2E, F, J and K).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of CCL2 in plasma from FPR2 KO vs WT C57BL/6 mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Parameters such as haematocrit and vascular leakage returned to basal levels 72 hr after infection in WT animals but persisted at elevated levels in KO animals.
source: While parameters, such as haematocrit and vascular leakage, returned to basal levels 72 hr after infection in WT animals, KO animals persisted with elevated levels, indicating a delay in resolving the host's haematological and immune response.
evidence: Supported by time-course measurements of haematocrit and vascular leakage in WT vs KO mice shown in Figure 2C-D and 2H-I.

claim: AnxA1 KO animals have a delay in resolving the host's haematological and immune response to DENV infection.
source: While parameters, such as haematocrit and vascular leakage, returned to basal levels 72 hr after infection in WT animals, KO animals persisted with elevated levels, indicating a delay in resolving the host's haematological and immune response.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that disease parameters persist longer in KO animals compared to WT animals.

claim: AnxA1-depleted animals preserved their ability to control virus spread.
source: Interestingly, AnxA1-depleted animals have preserved their ability to control virus spread, as splenic virus replication was similar to what was found in control animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR quantification of DENV genome copies in spleen of AnxA1 KO vs WT mice (n=4), shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Splenic virus replication was similar between AnxA1 KO and WT control animals.
source: Interestingly, AnxA1-depleted animals have preserved their ability to control virus spread, as splenic virus replication was similar to what was found in control animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR quantification of DENV genome copies in spleen shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 protected against thrombocytopenia in DENV-infected WT animals.
source: Thrombocytopenia (Figure 3B) and haemoconcentration (Figure 3C) were significantly milder in the group treated with Ac2-26.
evidence: Supported by platelet count measurements in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated BALB/c WT mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 protected against haemoconcentration in DENV-infected WT animals.
source: Thrombocytopenia (Figure 3B) and haemoconcentration (Figure 3C) were significantly milder in the group treated with Ac2-26.
evidence: Supported by haematocrit measurements in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated BALB/c WT mice after DENV-2 infection (n=4-5), shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 reduced vascular permeability in DENV-infected WT animals.
source: DENV-2 infection provoked increased vascular permeability in both untreated and treated animals, but to a lesser extent when animals were administrated daily with AnxA1 mimetic peptide (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by Evans blue vascular leakage assay in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated BALB/c WT mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 delayed the onset of increased haematocrit levels in DENV-infected mice.
source: Of note, whilst increased haematocrit levels and vascular leakage were observed as early as 24-hr post-infection in vehicle-treated mice, treatment with AnxA1 mimetic peptide delayed the onset of both disease manifestations (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by time-course haematocrit measurements comparing Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated mice shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 delayed the onset of vascular leakage in DENV-infected mice.
source: Of note, whilst increased haematocrit levels and vascular leakage were observed as early as 24-hr post-infection in vehicle-treated mice, treatment with AnxA1 mimetic peptide delayed the onset of both disease manifestations (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by time-course vascular leakage measurements comparing Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated mice shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 reduced plasma MCPT-1 levels in DENV-infected WT animals.
source: Treatment with Ac2-26 also reduced the elevation in plasma MCPT-1 (Figure 3E) and CCL2 (Figure 3F) levels compared to the untreated group.
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of MCPT-1 in plasma from Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated BALB/c WT mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 reduced plasma CCL2 levels in DENV-infected WT animals.
source: Treatment with Ac2-26 also reduced the elevation in plasma MCPT-1 (Figure 3E) and CCL2 (Figure 3F) levels compared to the untreated group.
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of CCL2 in plasma from Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated BALB/c WT mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The improvements in disease symptoms with Ac2-26 treatment appeared to be independent of splenic viral load.
source: Notably, the improvements in disease symptoms appeared to be independent of the splenic viral load (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR quantification of DENV genome copies in spleen of Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated BALB/c WT mice (n=4), shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ac2-26 did not affect disease parameters in FPR2 KO mice infected with DENV-2.
source: When we applied the same treatment schedule to FPR2 KO mice infected with DENV-2, Ac2-26 did not affect the disease parameters under observation (Figure 3G–K).
evidence: Supported by measurements of thrombocytopenia, haemoconcentration, vascular permeability, MCPT-1, and CCL2 in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated FPR2 KO mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 3G-K.

claim: Administration of Ac2-26 to AnxA1 KO mice rescued the phenotype showed by this transgenic colony in dengue infection.
source: Finally, the efficacy of Ac2-26 in these settings allowed us to validate the data obtained with AnxA1 KO mice, as administration of AnxA1 peptide to animals deficient in AnxA1 rescued the phenotype showed by this transgenic colony in dengue infection, bringing values of haematological and immune parameters in line with those measured in untreated mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by measurements of disease parameters in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated AnxA1 KO mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: DENV-infected A129 mice showed reduced AnxA1 plasma levels over the course of infection compared with mock-infected animals.
source: As seen for BALB/c and C57BL/6 strains, DENV-infected A129 mice showed reduced AnxA1 plasma levels over the course of infection, compared with mock-infected animals (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of plasma AnxA1 at multiple time points after DENV-2 infection in A129 mice (n=5), shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Untreated A129 mice lost approximately 10% of their body weight from day 2 post-infection until the last time point analysed.
source: While untreated A129 mice lost ~10% of their body weight from day 2 post-infection until the last time point analysed, treatment with Ac2-26 substantially delayed weight loss onset (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements in vehicle-treated A129 mice after DENV-2 infection (n=4-8), shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 substantially delayed weight loss onset in DENV-infected A129 mice.
source: While untreated A129 mice lost ~10% of their body weight from day 2 post-infection until the last time point analysed, treatment with Ac2-26 substantially delayed weight loss onset (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements comparing Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice after DENV-2 infection (n=4-8), shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ac2-26 significantly reduced thrombocytopenia in DENV-infected A129 mice.
source: The AnxA1 mimetic significantly reduced thrombocytopenia and haemoconcentration in response to DENV infection (Figure 4D and E) and displayed efficacy on controlling innate immunity mediators, with more significant effects in spleen values rather than plasma levels for CCL5 and IL-6 (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Supported by platelet count measurements in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5-14), shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Ac2-26 significantly reduced haemoconcentration in DENV-infected A129 mice.
source: The AnxA1 mimetic significantly reduced thrombocytopenia and haemoconcentration in response to DENV infection (Figure 4D and E) and displayed efficacy on controlling innate immunity mediators, with more significant effects in spleen values rather than plasma levels for CCL5 and IL-6 (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Supported by haematocrit measurements in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice after DENV-2 infection (n=8), shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Ac2-26 displayed efficacy on controlling innate immunity mediators, with more significant effects in spleen values rather than plasma levels for CCL5 and IL-6.
source: The AnxA1 mimetic significantly reduced thrombocytopenia and haemoconcentration in response to DENV infection (Figure 4D and E) and displayed efficacy on controlling innate immunity mediators, with more significant effects in spleen values rather than plasma levels for CCL5 and IL-6 (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of CCL5 and IL-6 in plasma and spleen from Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice after DENV-2 infection (CCL5 n=4-7; IL-6 n=4-13), shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Ac2-26 attenuated the systemic release of MCPT-1 induced by DENV-2 in A129 mice.
source: As observed in immunocompetent mice, Ac2-26 attenuated the systemic release of MCPT-1 induced by DENV-2 (Figure 4H), although it did not affect systemic levels of CCL2 (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of MCPT-1 in plasma from Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Ac2-26 did not affect systemic levels of CCL2 in DENV-infected A129 mice.
source: As observed in immunocompetent mice, Ac2-26 attenuated the systemic release of MCPT-1 induced by DENV-2 (Figure 4H), although it did not affect systemic levels of CCL2 (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of CCL2 in plasma from Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Infection of A129 mice induced liver damage, monitored by elevated plasma levels of ALT and high-histopathological score.
source: Infection of A129 mice induced a degree of liver damage, monitored by elevated plasma levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and high-histopathological score (Figure 4J–K).
evidence: Supported by ALT measurements and histopathological scoring in DENV-2-infected vs mock-infected A129 mice (n=4-8), shown in Figure 4J-L.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 attenuated liver injury caused by DENV in A129 mice.
source: Remarkably, treatment with Ac2-26 attenuated liver injury caused by DENV, as indicated by reduced histopathological score (Figure 4J and K) and ALT transaminase levels (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by histopathological scoring and ALT measurements in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice after DENV-2 infection (n=4-8), shown in Figure 4J-L.

claim: Ac2-26 alone (in the absence of infection) did not cause any notable adverse effects, impacted inflammatory and haematological parameters, or caused liver damage.
source: Ac2-26 alone (in the absence of infection) did not cause any notable adverse effects, impacted inflammatory and haematological parameters, or caused liver damage (Figure 4C–I and L).
evidence: Supported by measurements in mock-infected A129 mice treated with Ac2-26 vs vehicle, shown in Figure 4C-I and L.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 caused a significant reduction in haematological alterations induced by DENV-1, DENV-3, or DENV-4 in A129 mice.
source: In this animal strain and using this protocol, we could test the effects of Ac2-26 following infection with other DENV serotypes and observed a significant reduction in haematological alterations, liver damage, and IL-6 production induced by either DENV-1, DENV-3, or DENV-4 (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by platelet counts and haematocrit measurements in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice infected with DENV-1, DENV-3, or DENV-4 (n=5), shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 caused a significant reduction in liver damage induced by DENV-1, DENV-3, or DENV-4 in A129 mice.
source: In this animal strain and using this protocol, we could test the effects of Ac2-26 following infection with other DENV serotypes and observed a significant reduction in haematological alterations, liver damage, and IL-6 production induced by either DENV-1, DENV-3, or DENV-4 (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by ALT measurements in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice infected with DENV-1, DENV-3, or DENV-4 (n=5), shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 caused a significant reduction in IL-6 production induced by DENV-1, DENV-3, or DENV-4 in A129 mice.
source: In this animal strain and using this protocol, we could test the effects of Ac2-26 following infection with other DENV serotypes and observed a significant reduction in haematological alterations, liver damage, and IL-6 production induced by either DENV-1, DENV-3, or DENV-4 (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of IL-6 in plasma and spleen from Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice infected with DENV-1, DENV-3, or DENV-4 (n=5), shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: A129 mice showed systemic viral burden on day five after DENV1-4 inoculation, with detectable viremia and viral load in spleen and liver.
source: A129 mice showed systemic viral burden on day five after DENV1-4 inoculation, with detectable viremia and viral load in spleen and liver (Figures 4M, 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by plaque assay measurements of viral loads in plasma, spleen, and liver from A129 mice infected with DENV-1, -2, -3, or -4 (n=5-8), shown in Figures 4M and 5F-G.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 did not affect systemic viral burden in A129 mice, as untreated and treated mice showed similar viremia and viral loads.
source: Treatment with Ac2-26 did not affect systemic viral burden, as untreated and treated mice showed similar viremia and viral loads.
evidence: Supported by plaque assay measurements comparing viral loads in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice infected with DENV-1, -2, -3, or -4, shown in Figures 4M and 5F-G.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 caused only a slight reduction in viral loads in the spleen of mice infected with DENV-2.
source: Treatment with Ac2-26 caused only a slight reduction in viral loads in the spleen of mice infected with DENV-2 (Figure 4M) and in the plasma of animals inoculated with DENV-3 (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by plaque assay measurements of splenic viral loads in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice infected with DENV-2 (n=8), shown in Figure 4M.

claim: Treatment with Ac2-26 caused only a slight reduction in viral loads in the plasma of animals inoculated with DENV-3.
source: Treatment with Ac2-26 caused only a slight reduction in viral loads in the spleen of mice infected with DENV-2 (Figure 4M) and in the plasma of animals inoculated with DENV-3 (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by plaque assay measurements of plasma viral loads in Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated A129 mice infected with DENV-3 (n=5), shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The AnxA1 mimetic positively impacts severe dengue model, exerting little or no control on virus dissemination and viral loads, thus genuinely regulating the host response.
source: These data indicate that the AnxA1 mimetic positively impacts this severe dengue model, exerting little or no control on virus dissemination and viral loads, thus genuinely regulating the host response.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ac2-26 improves disease parameters without significantly affecting viral loads in A129 mice.

claim: The efficacy of the AnxA1 peptide is not restricted to a single virus serotype.
source: Moreover, we show that the efficacy of the AnxA1 peptide is not restricted to a single virus serotype.
evidence: Supported by data showing Ac2-26 efficacy against DENV-1, -2, -3, and -4 in A129 mice, shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Mast cell degranulation contributes to DENV-induced vascular leakage and disease severity.
source: There is compelling evidence that mast cell (MC) degranulation contributes to DENV-induced vascular leakage and disease severity (St John et al., 2013b; Syenina et al., 2015; Tissera et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications demonstrating the role of MC degranulation in dengue pathology.

claim: Increased MCPT-1 levels in the plasma of DENV-infected mice are enhanced in the absence of functional AnxA1/FPR2.
source: In line with this, we report increased MCPT-1 levels in the plasma of DENV-infected mice, which is enhanced in the absence of functional AnxA1/FPR2 and is counterbalanced by AnxA1 peptide treatment (Figure 2E and J; Figure 3E, J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of MCPT-1 in plasma from AnxA1 KO and FPR2 KO mice after DENV infection, shown in Figures 2E, 2J, 3E, 3J, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Increased MCPT-1 levels in the plasma of DENV-infected mice are counterbalanced by AnxA1 peptide treatment.
source: In line with this, we report increased MCPT-1 levels in the plasma of DENV-infected mice, which is enhanced in the absence of functional AnxA1/FPR2 and is counterbalanced by AnxA1 peptide treatment (Figure 2E and J; Figure 3E, J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of MCPT-1 in plasma from Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated mice after DENV infection, shown in Figures 3E, 3J, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Both local and systemic administration of Ac2-26 decreased MC degranulation in DENV-infected WT mice.
source: We first analysed MCs from hind paw histological sections of WT mice pretreated with vehicle or AnxA1 mimetic peptide and infected with DENV (Figure 6A). Both animals treated locally or systemically had decreased MC degranulation in comparison with control mice.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of MC degranulation in hind paw sections from Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated BALB/c WT mice after DENV-2 infection (n=6), shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Systemic administration of Ac2-26 prevents mast cell degranulation in vivo.
source: After verifying that systemic administration of Ac2-26 prevents mast cell degranulation in vivo, we subjected AnxA1 KO and FPR2 KO mice to the same challenge and treatment schedule (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of MC degranulation in hind paw sections from systemically Ac2-26-treated mice, shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ac2-26 successfully reduces mast cell degranulation in AnxA1 KO mice.
source: We verified that Ac2-26 successfully reduces mast cell degranulation in AnxA1 KO mice (Figure 6B) but failed to rescue DENV-induced degranulation in FPR2 KO mice (Figure 6C), confirming the dependence of this receptor for its therapeutic actions.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of MC degranulation in hind paw sections from Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated AnxA1 KO mice after DENV-2 infection (n=5), shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Ac2-26 failed to rescue DENV-induced degranulation in FPR2 KO mice.
source: We verified that Ac2-26 successfully reduces mast cell degranulation in AnxA1 KO mice (Figure 6B) but failed to rescue DENV-induced degranulation in FPR2 KO mice (Figure 6C), confirming the dependence of this receptor for its therapeutic actions.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of MC degranulation in hind paw sections from Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated FPR2 KO mice after DENV-2 infection (n=4-5), shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The therapeutic actions of Ac2-26 are dependent on FPR2 receptor.
source: We verified that Ac2-26 successfully reduces mast cell degranulation in AnxA1 KO mice (Figure 6B) but failed to rescue DENV-induced degranulation in FPR2 KO mice (Figure 6C), confirming the dependence of this receptor for its therapeutic actions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ac2-26 is effective in AnxA1 KO mice but not in FPR2 KO mice.

claim: The absence of FPR2 significantly increased mast cell degranulation in response to local challenge with DENV compared to WT counterparts.
source: Notably, the absence of FPR2 significantly increased mast cell degranulation in response to the local challenge with DENV compared to the WT counterparts (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of MC degranulation comparing FPR2 KO vs WT C57BL/6 mice after DENV-2 infection, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ac2-26 inhibited β-hexosaminidase release evoked by DENV-2 in a concentration-dependent manner in BMMCs.
source: Ac2-26 inhibited β-hexosaminidase release evoked by DENV-2 in a concentration-dependent manner, with ~40% reduction in release at 100 µM Ac2-26 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by β-hexosaminidase assay in BMMCs pretreated with increasing concentrations of Ac2-26 and stimulated with DENV-2 (n=4), shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Ac2-26 at 100 µM caused approximately 40% reduction in β-hexosaminidase release from BMMCs stimulated with DENV-2.
source: Ac2-26 inhibited β-hexosaminidase release evoked by DENV-2 in a concentration-dependent manner, with ~40% reduction in release at 100 µM Ac2-26 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by β-hexosaminidase assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: DENV infection caused enlarged cytoplasmic granules with reduced electron density in BMMCs.
source: Ultrastructural evidence of degranulation was identified in BMMC cultured with DENV (Figure 6H and J), in which cells showed enlarged cytoplasmic granules with reduced electron density and granule–granule fusion events – all morphological changes indicative of content release (Carmo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy analysis of BMMCs stimulated with DENV-2, shown in Figure 6H and J.

claim: DENV infection caused granule-granule fusion events in BMMCs.
source: Ultrastructural evidence of degranulation was identified in BMMC cultured with DENV (Figure 6H and J), in which cells showed enlarged cytoplasmic granules with reduced electron density and granule–granule fusion events – all morphological changes indicative of content release (Carmo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy analysis of BMMCs stimulated with DENV-2, shown in Figure 6H and J.

claim: Enlarged cytoplasmic granules with reduced electron density and granule-granule fusion events are morphological changes indicative of content release in mast cells.
source: Ultrastructural evidence of degranulation was identified in BMMC cultured with DENV (Figure 6H and J), in which cells showed enlarged cytoplasmic granules with reduced electron density and granule–granule fusion events – all morphological changes indicative of content release (Carmo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous publication and TEM observations in the current study.

claim: Morphological features of degranulation were consistently reduced when DENV-infected BMMCs were pretreated with 100 µM Ac2-26 peptide.
source: These features were consistently reduced when infected cells were pretreated with 100 µM Ac2-26 peptide (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy analysis of BMMCs pretreated with Ac2-26 and stimulated with DENV-2, shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Ac2-26 prevented the increase in granule diameters caused by DENV in BMMCs.
source: Quantification of the morphological changes in granules showed that Ac2-26 prevented the increase in granule diameters caused by DENV (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative TEM analysis of granule diameters in BMMCs (372, 360, and 384 granules analysed in mock, DENV-2, and DENV-2+Ac2-26 groups, respectively), shown in Figure 6E.

claim: DENV infection caused a significant increase in the number of granule-granule fusions in BMMCs compared to mock-stimulated group.
source: In addition, quantitative TEM demonstrated a significant increase in the number of granule-granule fusions in response to DENV infection than the mock-stimulated group; a feature significantly attenuated upon Ac2-26 pre-treatment (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative TEM analysis of fused granules in 15 sections per group, shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Ac2-26 pre-treatment significantly attenuated the increase in granule-granule fusions caused by DENV infection in BMMCs.
source: In addition, quantitative TEM demonstrated a significant increase in the number of granule-granule fusions in response to DENV infection than the mock-stimulated group; a feature significantly attenuated upon Ac2-26 pre-treatment (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative TEM analysis of fused granules in 15 sections per group, shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The AnxA1 mimetic peptide Ac2-26 directly acts on MC diminishing its degranulation in response to DENV.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that the AnxA1 mimetic peptide Ac2-26 directly acts on MC diminishing its degranulation in response to DENV.
evidence: Inferred from in vitro β-hexosaminidase assay and TEM data showing Ac2-26 reduces DENV-induced MC degranulation.

claim: An inadequate engagement of the resolution circuit AnxA1-FPR2/ALX may contribute to dengue infection's pathogenesis with particular relevance for the cohort of patients affected by the most severe forms of the disease.
source: We present evidence that an inadequate engagement of the resolution circuit AnxA1-FPR2/ALX may contribute to dengue infection's pathogenesis with particular relevance for the cohort of patients affected by the most severe forms of the disease.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that AnxA1 is reduced in severe dengue patients and that disruption of the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway worsens disease in mice.

claim: Depletion of the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway aggravates clinical signs associated with DENV infection.
source: We have identified that: (i) AnxA1 is downregulated in the plasma of dengue patients in comparison to healthy individuals and in DENV-infected mice in comparison to non-infected animals; (ii) depletion of the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway aggravates clinical signs and enhances MC activation associated to DENV infection, indicating a nonredundant role for this resolution pathway in the pathogenesis of dengue disease
evidence: Supported by data from AnxA1 KO and FPR2 KO mice showing worse disease parameters after DENV infection.

claim: Depletion of the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway enhances MC activation associated with DENV infection.
source: We have identified that: (i) AnxA1 is downregulated in the plasma of dengue patients in comparison to healthy individuals and in DENV-infected mice in comparison to non-infected animals; (ii) depletion of the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway aggravates clinical signs and enhances MC activation associated to DENV infection, indicating a nonredundant role for this resolution pathway in the pathogenesis of dengue disease
evidence: Supported by increased MCPT-1 levels and histological evidence of increased MC degranulation in AnxA1 KO and FPR2 KO mice after DENV infection.

claim: The AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway plays a nonredundant role in the pathogenesis of dengue disease.
source: We have identified that: (i) AnxA1 is downregulated in the plasma of dengue patients in comparison to healthy individuals and in DENV-infected mice in comparison to non-infected animals; (ii) depletion of the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway aggravates clinical signs and enhances MC activation associated to DENV infection, indicating a nonredundant role for this resolution pathway in the pathogenesis of dengue disease
evidence: Inferred from the observation that genetic deletion of either AnxA1 or FPR2 worsens dengue disease.

claim: Pharmacological treatment of mice with an FPR2/ALX agonistic peptide produced beneficial effects during DENV infection.
source: We have identified that: (i) AnxA1 is downregulated in the plasma of dengue patients in comparison to healthy individuals and in DENV-infected mice in comparison to non-infected animals; (ii) depletion of the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway aggravates clinical signs and enhances MC activation associated to DENV infection, indicating a nonredundant role for this resolution pathway in the pathogenesis of dengue disease; (iii) pharmacological treatment of mice with an FPR2/ALX agonistic peptide produced beneficial effects during DENV infection
evidence: Supported by data showing Ac2-26 treatment reduces disease parameters in multiple mouse models of DENV infection.

claim: AnxA1 mimetic peptide has direct inhibitory effects on MC degranulation induced by DENV.
source: We have identified that: (i) AnxA1 is downregulated in the plasma of dengue patients in comparison to healthy individuals and in DENV-infected mice in comparison to non-infected animals; (ii) depletion of the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway aggravates clinical signs and enhances MC activation associated to DENV infection, indicating a nonredundant role for this resolution pathway in the pathogenesis of dengue disease; (iii) pharmacological treatment of mice with an FPR2/ALX agonistic peptide produced beneficial effects during DENV infection; (iv) AnxA1 mimetic peptide has direct inhibitory effects on MC degranulation induced by DENV
evidence: Supported by in vitro β-hexosaminidase assay and TEM data showing Ac2-26 reduces DENV-induced MC degranulation.

claim: AnxA1 mimetic peptide does not significantly control viral load and virus dissemination.
source: We have identified that: (i) AnxA1 is downregulated in the plasma of dengue patients in comparison to healthy individuals and in DENV-infected mice in comparison to non-infected animals; (ii) depletion of the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway aggravates clinical signs and enhances MC activation associated to DENV infection, indicating a nonredundant role for this resolution pathway in the pathogenesis of dengue disease; (iii) pharmacological treatment of mice with an FPR2/ALX agonistic peptide produced beneficial effects during DENV infection; (iv) AnxA1 mimetic peptide has direct inhibitory effects on MC degranulation induced by DENV while (v) it does not seem to control viral load and virus dissemination significantly.
evidence: Supported by viral load measurements showing no significant difference between Ac2-26-treated and vehicle-treated mice in multiple models.

claim: Dengue is caused by one of four serotypes of dengue virus (DENV1-4) transmitted by Aedes Aegypti and A. Albopictus mosquitoes.
source: Dengue is caused by one of four serotypes of dengue virus (DENV1-4) transmitted by Aedes Aegypti and A. Albopictus mosquitoes, affecting around 400 million people in 128 countries (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to epidemiological study.

claim: Dengue affects around 400 million people in 128 countries.
source: Dengue is caused by one of four serotypes of dengue virus (DENV1-4) transmitted by Aedes Aegypti and A. Albopictus mosquitoes, affecting around 400 million people in 128 countries (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to epidemiological study.

claim: Severe dengue is typified by exacerbated systemic inflammation, vascular leakage, fluid accumulation, respiratory distress, severe bleeding, and/or organ impairment.
source: Occasionally, dengue infection develops into a potentially lethal complication identified as severe dengue, typified by exacerbated systemic inflammation, vascular leakage, fluid accumulation, respiratory distress, severe bleeding, and/or organ impairment (WHO, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO guidelines and established clinical knowledge.

claim: No antiviral drug for dengue treatment is available.
source: No antiviral drug for dengue treatment is available, and the use of Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV), the first dengue vaccine approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, has its limitations, such as the increased risk for development of severe dengue in the immune populations (Huang et al., 2021; WHO, 2018; The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations and established clinical knowledge.

claim: Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV) is the first dengue vaccine approved by the US Food and Drug Administration.
source: No antiviral drug for dengue treatment is available, and the use of Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV), the first dengue vaccine approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, has its limitations, such as the increased risk for development of severe dengue in the immune populations (Huang et al., 2021; WHO, 2018; The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations and established knowledge.

claim: Dengvaxia has limitations, such as the increased risk for development of severe dengue in immune populations.
source: No antiviral drug for dengue treatment is available, and the use of Dengvaxia (CYD-TDV), the first dengue vaccine approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, has its limitations, such as the increased risk for development of severe dengue in the immune populations (Huang et al., 2021; WHO, 2018; The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to publications documenting vaccine safety concerns.

claim: Dengue is a major unmet clinical problem in countries affected by this disease.
source: Thus, the combination of these factors points to dengue as a major unmet clinical problem in countries affected by this disease (Shepard et al., 2016; Stanaway et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effective treatments and vaccine limitations, supported by citations.

claim: The pathogenesis of severe dengue results from exacerbated host innate and adaptative immune responses to DENV.
source: The pathogenesis of severe dengue results from exacerbated host innate and adaptative immune responses to DENV.
evidence: Supported by established scientific understanding and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mast cells lining blood vessels are target cells for DENV in humans.
source: Among the target cells for DENV in humans, mast cells (MCs) lining blood vessels undergo dramatic cellular activation in response to DENV, despite their high resistance to infection (; St John et al., 2013bSt John et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Mast cells undergo dramatic cellular activation in response to DENV, despite their high resistance to infection.
source: Among the target cells for DENV in humans, mast cells (MCs) lining blood vessels undergo dramatic cellular activation in response to DENV, despite their high resistance to infection (; St John et al., 2013bSt John et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: MC activation evoked by DENV triggers the production of inflammatory cytokines (cytokine storm) and vascular leakage.
source: As essential regulators of vascular integrity, MC activation evoked by DENV triggers the production of inflammatory cytokines (cytokine storm) and vascular leakage, which ultimately result in hypovolemic shock in severe dengue (St John et al., 2013b; Syenina et al., 2015St John et al., 2011;).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: MC activation evoked by DENV ultimately results in hypovolemic shock in severe dengue.
source: As essential regulators of vascular integrity, MC activation evoked by DENV triggers the production of inflammatory cytokines (cytokine storm) and vascular leakage, which ultimately result in hypovolemic shock in severe dengue (St John et al., 2013b; Syenina et al., 2015St John et al., 2011;).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications and established pathophysiological understanding.

claim: There is a positive correlation between circulating chymase levels and disease severity in paediatric and adult dengue patients.
source: This is substantiated by a positive correlation between circulating chymase levels and disease severity recently observed in paediatric and adult patients (Rathore et al., 2020; Tissera et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Pharmacological suppression of inflammation has shown to be beneficial in experimental dengue.
source: In line with the suggested role of uncontrolled immune responses in the pathogenesis of DENV infection, pharmacological suppression of inflammation (Fu et al., 2014; Marques et al., 2015; Souza et al., 2009), MC stabilisation (St John et al., 2013bMorrison et al., 2017), and inhibition of MC-derived protease (Rathore et al., 2019) have shown to be beneficial in experimental dengue.
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: MC stabilisation has shown to be beneficial in experimental dengue.
source: In line with the suggested role of uncontrolled immune responses in the pathogenesis of DENV infection, pharmacological suppression of inflammation (Fu et al., 2014; Marques et al., 2015; Souza et al., 2009), MC stabilisation (St John et al., 2013bMorrison et al., 2017), and inhibition of MC-derived protease (Rathore et al., 2019) have shown to be beneficial in experimental dengue.
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Inhibition of MC-derived protease has shown to be beneficial in experimental dengue.
source: In line with the suggested role of uncontrolled immune responses in the pathogenesis of DENV infection, pharmacological suppression of inflammation (Fu et al., 2014; Marques et al., 2015; Souza et al., 2009), MC stabilisation (St John et al., 2013bMorrison et al., 2017), and inhibition of MC-derived protease (Rathore et al., 2019) have shown to be beneficial in experimental dengue.
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Host-directed therapies targeting excessive or misplaced inflammation may be a viable approach in treating severe dengue infection.
source: These studies provide proof-of-concept that host-directed therapies targeting excessive or misplaced inflammation may be a viable approach in treating severe dengue infection.
evidence: Inferred from the beneficial effects of anti-inflammatory interventions in experimental dengue, supported by citations.

claim: Pro-resolving mediators are cell signalling molecules synthesised in a strict temporal and spatial fashion to regulate the host response and prevent excessive acute inflammatory reaction.
source: Pro-resolving mediators are cell signalling molecules synthesised in a strict temporal and spatial fashion to regulate the host response and prevent the excessive acute inflammatory reaction that damages the host (Sugimoto et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation and established knowledge in resolution biology.

claim: Dysregulation or 'failure' in pro-resolving mechanisms might be involved in the pathogenesis of several chronic inflammatory disorders.
source: The discovery of this active phase of inflammation has led to a new awareness of how a disease can emerge, including the concept that dysregulation or 'failure' in pro-resolving mechanisms might be involved in the pathogenesis of several chronic inflammatory disorders (Eke Gungor et al., 2014; Fredman et al., 2016; Murri et al., 2013; Schett and Neurath, 2018; Sena et al., 2013; Thul et al., 2017; Vong et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to publications on resolution failure in various diseases.

claim: AnxA1 and its cognate receptor FPR2/ALX bear anti-inflammatory properties in sterile settings.
source: The pro-resolving protein Annexin A1 (AnxA1) and its cognate receptor formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2), also known as FPR2/lipoxin A4 receptor (FPR2/ALX), bear anti-inflammatory properties in sterile settings (Fredman et al., 2015; Galvão et al., 2017; Gimenes et al., 2015; Kusters et al., 2015; Leoni et al., 2015; Locatelli et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: AnxA1 and FPR2/ALX exert a degree of protection in experimental tuberculosis.
source: The pro-resolving protein Annexin A1 (AnxA1) and its cognate receptor formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2), also known as FPR2/lipoxin A4 receptor (FPR2/ALX), bear anti-inflammatory properties in sterile settings (Fredman et al., 2015; Galvão et al., 2017; Gimenes et al., 2015; Kusters et al., 2015; Leoni et al., 2015; Locatelli et al., 2014), and exert a degree of protection in infectious settings, such as experimental tuberculosis (Tzelepis et al., 2015; Vanessa et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: AnxA1 and FPR2/ALX exert a degree of protection in sepsis.
source: The pro-resolving protein Annexin A1 (AnxA1) and its cognate receptor formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2), also known as FPR2/lipoxin A4 receptor (FPR2/ALX), bear anti-inflammatory properties in sterile settings (Fredman et al., 2015; Galvão et al., 2017; Gimenes et al., 2015; Kusters et al., 2015; Leoni et al., 2015; Locatelli et al., 2014), and exert a degree of protection in infectious settings, such as experimental tuberculosis (Tzelepis et al., 2015; Vanessa et al., 2015), sepsis (Damazo et al., 2005; Gobbetti et al., 2014) Spite et al., 2009
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: AnxA1 and FPR2/ALX exert a degree of protection in pneumococcal pneumonia.
source: The pro-resolving protein Annexin A1 (AnxA1) and its cognate receptor formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2), also known as FPR2/lipoxin A4 receptor (FPR2/ALX), bear anti-inflammatory properties in sterile settings (Fredman et al., 2015; Galvão et al., 2017; Gimenes et al., 2015; Kusters et al., 2015; Leoni et al., 2015; Locatelli et al., 2014), and exert a degree of protection in infectious settings, such as experimental tuberculosis (Tzelepis et al., 2015; Vanessa et al., 2015), sepsis (Damazo et al., 2005; Gobbetti et al., 2014) Spite et al., 2009, pneumococcal pneumonia (Machado et al., 2020; Tavares et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: AnxA1 and FPR2/ALX exert a degree of protection in influenza.
source: The pro-resolving protein Annexin A1 (AnxA1) and its cognate receptor formyl peptide receptor 2 (FPR2), also known as FPR2/lipoxin A4 receptor (FPR2/ALX), bear anti-inflammatory properties in sterile settings (Fredman et al., 2015; Galvão et al., 2017; Gimenes et al., 2015; Kusters et al., 2015; Leoni et al., 2015; Locatelli et al., 2014), and exert a degree of protection in infectious settings, such as experimental tuberculosis (Tzelepis et al., 2015; Vanessa et al., 2015), sepsis (Damazo et al., 2005; Gobbetti et al., 2014) Spite et al., 2009, pneumococcal pneumonia (Machado et al., 2020; Tavares et al., 2016), and influenza (Schloer et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: AnxA1 acts as an endogenous modulator of MC degranulation in response to IgE/anti-IgE or compound 48/80.
source: AnxA1 has been recently described to act as an endogenous modulator of MC degranulation in response to IgE/anti-IgE or compound 48/80 (Parisi et al., 2019; Sinniah et al., 2019; Sinniah et al., 2016; Yazid et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: AnxA1 is well known to counter regulate overexuberant pro-inflammatory events and MC activation.
source: Since AnxA1 is well known to counter regulate overexuberant pro-inflammatory events and MC activation, we have hypothesised that an imbalance between this anti-inflammatory/pro-resolving mediator and pro-inflammatory molecules could be operating during dengue infection.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Studies on bacterial infection consistently revealed the ability of specialised pro-resolving mediators and AnxA1 to facilitate innate immune responses against the pathogen whilst reducing the harmful effects of inflammation.
source: Whilst studies on bacterial infection consistently revealed the ability of specialised pro-resolving mediators and AnxA1 (Chiang et al., 2012; Decker et al., 2021; Gobbetti et al., 2014; Machado et al., 2020; Sekheri et al., 2020; Tzelepis et al., 2015; Vanessa et al., 2015) to facilitate innate immune responses against the pathogen whilst reducing the harmful effects of inflammation, the translational potential of these results to viral infection was less clear.
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies on bacterial infections.

claim: The translational potential of pro-resolving mediator results from bacterial infection to viral infection was less clear.
source: Whilst studies on bacterial infection consistently revealed the ability of specialised pro-resolving mediators and AnxA1 (Chiang et al., 2012; Decker et al., 2021; Gobbetti et al., 2014; Machado et al., 2020; Sekheri et al., 2020; Tzelepis et al., 2015; Vanessa et al., 2015) to facilitate innate immune responses against the pathogen whilst reducing the harmful effects of inflammation, the translational potential of these results to viral infection was less clear.
evidence: Inferred from the statement that bacterial infection studies were more established than viral infection studies for pro-resolving mediators.

claim: Failure to trigger the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX molecular pathway may contribute to disease severity in dengue infection.
source: Our results suggest that failure to trigger this molecular pathway may contribute to disease severity in dengue infection and support the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway as a potential target for host-directed therapy in human dengue disease.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that AnxA1 is reduced in severe dengue and that disruption of the pathway worsens disease.

claim: The AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway is a potential target for host-directed therapy in human dengue disease.
source: Our results suggest that failure to trigger this molecular pathway may contribute to disease severity in dengue infection and support the AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway as a potential target for host-directed therapy in human dengue disease.
evidence: Inferred from the therapeutic efficacy of Ac2-26 in experimental dengue models.

claim: All patients with positive PCR reactions were infected with DENV-1.
source: All patients with positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) reactions were infected with DENV-1, in line with a report that DENV-1 was the predominant serotype circulating in the city in which patients were recruited in the years of sample collection (Gonçalves Pereira et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data from patient samples and citation to epidemiological report.

claim: DENV-1 was the predominant serotype circulating in the city in which patients were recruited in the years of sample collection.
source: All patients with positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) reactions were infected with DENV-1, in line with a report that DENV-1 was the predominant serotype circulating in the city in which patients were recruited in the years of sample collection (Gonçalves Pereira et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to epidemiological report.

claim: The proportion of patients showing secondary dengue infection was not significantly different between the non-SD and SD groups.
source: The proportion of patients showing secondary dengue infection was not significantly different between the non-SD and SD groups.
evidence: Supported by analysis of patient data shown in Table 1.

claim: The severe dengue cohort was characterised by increased age compared to non-severe dengue patients.
source: In line with the association between older age in adults and an increased risk factor for progression to severe disease, our cohort was characterised by increased age in patients with SD (Rowe et al., 2014; Sangkaew et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by demographic data shown in Table 1 and citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Older age in adults is an increased risk factor for progression to severe dengue disease.
source: In line with the association between older age in adults and an increased risk factor for progression to severe disease, our cohort was characterised by increased age in patients with SD (Rowe et al., 2014; Sangkaew et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Wild-type mice are more resistant to DENV infection than immunocompromised animals.
source: Although wild-type (WT) mice are more resistant to infection than immunocompromised animals (Shresta et al., 2004); these animals were proven to be productively infected by DENV and are valid hosts to investigate the mechanisms underlying DENV-induced vascular dysfunction (Chen et al., 2007; St John et al., 2013b; Syenina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous publication.

claim: Wild-type mice are productively infected by DENV and are valid hosts to investigate the mechanisms underlying DENV-induced vascular dysfunction.
source: Although wild-type (WT) mice are more resistant to infection than immunocompromised animals (Shresta et al., 2004); these animals were proven to be productively infected by DENV and are valid hosts to investigate the mechanisms underlying DENV-induced vascular dysfunction (Chen et al., 2007; St John et al., 2013b; Syenina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Systemic infection of WT mice with DENV caused haematological and vascular changes consistent with human disease.
source: As previously described (St John et al., 2013b), systemic infection of WT mice caused haematological and vascular changes consistent with the human disease, systemic MC activation, and inflammatory response (Figure 2B–K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B-K and citation to previous publication.

claim: Systemic infection of WT mice with DENV caused systemic MC activation.
source: As previously described (St John et al., 2013b), systemic infection of WT mice caused haematological and vascular changes consistent with the human disease, systemic MC activation, and inflammatory response (Figure 2B–K).
evidence: Supported by MCPT-1 measurements shown in Figure 2E and 2J.

claim: Systemic infection of WT mice with DENV caused inflammatory response.
source: As previously described (St John et al., 2013b), systemic infection of WT mice caused haematological and vascular changes consistent with the human disease, systemic MC activation, and inflammatory response (Figure 2B–K).
evidence: Supported by CCL2 measurements shown in Figure 2F and 2K.

claim: A129 mice are highly susceptible to DENV infection.
source: To complement our studies with immunocompetent animals mice, we performed experiments in A129 mice since they are known to be very susceptible to flaviviruses infections (de Freitas et al., 2019; Del Sarto et al., 2020) and develop a more severe disease manifestation that emulates several features of severe dengue in humans (Zandi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: A129 mice develop a more severe disease manifestation that emulates several features of severe dengue in humans.
source: To complement our studies with immunocompetent animals mice, we performed experiments in A129 mice since they are known to be very susceptible to flaviviruses infections (de Freitas et al., 2019; Del Sarto et al., 2020) and develop a more severe disease manifestation that emulates several features of severe dengue in humans (Zandi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous publication.

claim: A129 mice are considered a gold standard viremia model to test potential antiviral therapies.
source: The later is considered a gold standard viremia model to test potential antiviral therapies (Meyts and Casanova, 2021; Williams et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Ac2-26 binds to FPR2/ALX and mimics most of the whole protein's effects in experimental inflammation.
source: Ac2-26 binds to FPR2/ALX and mimics most of the whole protein's effects in experimental inflammation (Sheikh and Solito, 2018; Sugimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: The peptide therapy with Ac2-26 in WT animals was effective after the first injection.
source: The peptide therapy in WT animals (Figure 3A) was effective after the first injection and protected against the major changes in haematological and immune markers as evident at 24 hr and 48 hr after DENV infection compared to mock-infected animals (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: Supported by data showing improvements in disease parameters at 24 hr and 48 hr after infection in Ac2-26-treated mice, shown in Figure 3B-F.

claim: Ac2-26 protected against major changes in haematological and immune markers at 24 hr and 48 hr after DENV infection.
source: The peptide therapy in WT animals (Figure 3A) was effective after the first injection and protected against the major changes in haematological and immune markers as evident at 24 hr and 48 hr after DENV infection compared to mock-infected animals (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: Supported by measurements of thrombocytopenia, haemoconcentration, vascular leakage, MCPT-1, and CCL2 shown in Figure 3B-F.

claim: Viremia is not detectable in immunocompetent mice infected with DENV.
source: Although viremia is not detectable in immunocompetent mice, we noticed transient viral RNA detection in the spleen starting 24 hr after infection, peaking at 48 hr or 72 hr, followed by disappearance at 96 hr, in line with previous studies using the same model (St John et al., 2013b; Syenina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge from previous studies and citations.

claim: Transient viral RNA is detected in the spleen of immunocompetent mice starting 24 hr after DENV infection, peaking at 48 hr or 72 hr, followed by disappearance at 96 hr.
source: Although viremia is not detectable in immunocompetent mice, we noticed transient viral RNA detection in the spleen starting 24 hr after infection, peaking at 48 hr or 72 hr, followed by disappearance at 96 hr, in line with previous studies using the same model (St John et al., 2013b; Syenina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data from spleen samples shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citations to previous studies.

claim: Neither genetic deletion of AnxA1 nor treatment with Ac2-26 affected the profile of viral RNA detection in the spleen of immunocompetent mice.
source: Neither genetic deletion of AnxA1 or treatment with Ac2-26 affected this profile.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data comparing viral RNA levels in AnxA1 KO vs WT mice and Ac2-26-treated vs vehicle-treated mice, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Plaque assay is the gold standard methodology to evaluate viable viral particles in vivo.
source: Therefore, in our study we show, by two different techniques, that is, quantification of viral RNA (immunocompetent mice) and quantification of viable particles (A129 mice), and in two different models (high and low DENV inoculums) that neither absence of AnxA1 nor treatment with peptide Ac2-26 interferes with the host ability to deal with the infection, despite its beneficial pro-resolving effects.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in virology.

claim: Neither absence of AnxA1 nor treatment with peptide Ac2-26 interferes with the host ability to deal with DENV infection, despite its beneficial pro-resolving effects.
source: Therefore, in our study we show, by two different techniques, that is, quantification of viral RNA (immunocompetent mice) and quantification of viable particles (A129 mice), and in two different models (high and low DENV inoculums) that neither absence of AnxA1 nor treatment with peptide Ac2-26 interferes with the host ability to deal with the infection, despite its beneficial pro-resolving effects.
evidence: Supported by viral load measurements in AnxA1 KO mice and Ac2-26-treated mice using both RT-PCR and plaque assay techniques.

claim: DENV infection initiates pro-inflammatory responses aiming to control virus spread that ultimately contributes to the immunopathology of dengue.
source: DENV infection initiates pro-inflammatory responses aiming to control virus spread that ultimately contributes to the immunopathology of dengue.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in dengue pathogenesis.

claim: MC activation in response to DENV plays an essential role in DENV-induced vascular pathology, particularly concerning the plasma leakage that causes hypovolemic shock in severe dengue.
source: For instance, MC activation in response to DENV plays an essential role in DENV-induced vascular pathology, particularly concerning the plasma leakage that causes hypovolemic shock in severe dengue (St John et al., 2013b; Syenina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: There is a correlation between circulating chymase levels and disease severity in dengue patients.
source: This is supported by a correlation between circulating chymase levels and disease severity in humans (Rathore et al., 2020; Tissera et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: AnxA1 acts as an endogenous modulator of MC degranulation in response to IgE/anti-IgE or compound 48/80, suggesting that this pro-resolving axis acts as a brake in MC degranulation.
source: It has been recently described that AnxA1 acts as an endogenous modulator of MC degranulation in response to IgE/anti-IgE or compound 48/80, suggesting that this pro-resolving axis act as a brake in MC degranulation (Sinniah et al., 2016; Yazid et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Ac2-26 reduces DENV-induced MC degranulation dose-dependently.
source: Herein, we have identified the ability of Ac2-26 to reduce DENV-induced MC degranulation dose-dependently, a mechanism that might underpin the reduced MCPT-1 secretion and vascular dysfunction observed in AnxA1 peptide-treated animals.
evidence: Supported by β-hexosaminidase assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The ability of Ac2-26 to reduce DENV-induced MC degranulation might underpin the reduced MCPT-1 secretion and vascular dysfunction observed in AnxA1 peptide-treated animals.
source: Herein, we have identified the ability of Ac2-26 to reduce DENV-induced MC degranulation dose-dependently, a mechanism that might underpin the reduced MCPT-1 secretion and vascular dysfunction observed in AnxA1 peptide-treated animals.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between reduced MC degranulation and improved disease parameters in Ac2-26-treated animals.

claim: In vivo and in vitro evidence suggest that Ac2-26 acts by attenuating MC degranulation evoked by DENV, protecting the host against vascular dysfunction associated with the disease.
source: Together, in vivo and in vitro evidence suggest that Ac2-26, at least in part, acts by attenuating MC degranulation evoked by DENV, protecting the host against vascular dysfunction associated with the disease.
evidence: Inferred from the combined in vivo and in vitro data showing Ac2-26 reduces MC degranulation and improves vascular parameters.

claim: The AnxA1-FPR2/ALX pathway is a relevant potential target for DENV infection treatment, as MCs are resistant to infection but play a key role in dengue pathogenesis.
source: This mode of action points to this pathway as a relevant potential target for DENV infection treatment, as MCs are resistant to infection but play a key role in dengue pathogenesis (; Rathore et al., 2019; Syenina et al., 2015; Tissera et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ac2-26 targets MC degranulation without affecting viral loads, and supported by citations on MC role in dengue.

claim: Recent studies have pointed towards a benefit of using corticoids in severe dengue with no significant adverse consequences or promotion of virus replication.
source: Although no therapy is available for dengue disease beyond supportive care, recent studies have pointed towards a benefit of using corticoids in severe dengue with no significant adverse consequences or promotion of virus replication (Bandara and Herath, 2018; Bandara and Herath, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Promotion of AnxA1 has shown to be relevant to the benefits afforded by glucocorticoids.
source: Amongst the several genomic and non-genomic actions of glucocorticoids (GC), promotion of AnxA1 has shown to be relevant to the benefits afforded by steroids (De Caterina et al., 1993; Solito et al., 2003), as suggested by the loss of the therapeutic effect of GC on AnxA1 depleted animals (Patel et al., 2012; Perretti and D'Acquisto, 2009; Vago et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Loss of the therapeutic effect of glucocorticoids occurs in AnxA1 depleted animals.
source: Amongst the several genomic and non-genomic actions of glucocorticoids (GC), promotion of AnxA1 has shown to be relevant to the benefits afforded by steroids (De Caterina et al., 1993; Solito et al., 2003), as suggested by the loss of the therapeutic effect of GC on AnxA1 depleted animals (Patel et al., 2012; Perretti and D'Acquisto, 2009; Vago et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The benefit of glucocorticoid in dengue disease could be partially attributed to promoting the glucocorticoid inducible Annexin A1-FPR2/ALX pathway.
source: Therefore, there is scope to hypothesise that the benefit of glucocorticoid in dengue disease could be partially attributed to promoting the glucocorticoid inducible Annexin A1-FPR2/ALX pathway.
evidence: Speculated based on the known relationship between glucocorticoids and AnxA1, and the findings of the current study.

claim: The use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents in dengue is discouraged, as they can increase the risk of bleeding.
source: Further investigation on GC and GC-inducible AnxA1 is particularly relevant in the context of dengue disease, where the use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents in dengue is discouraged, as they can increase the risk of bleeding (WHO, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO guidelines and established clinical knowledge.

claim: Altered levels of the pro-resolving mediator AnxA1 are of pathological relevance in dengue disease.
source: Our results indicate that altered levels of the pro-resolving mediator AnxA1 are of pathological relevance in dengue disease.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations that AnxA1 is reduced in dengue patients and that disruption of the pathway worsens disease in mice.

claim: Inadequate engagement of resolution circuits contributes to the excessive inflammation observed in severe DENV infection.
source: We show that inadequate engagement of resolution circuits contributes to the excessive inflammation observed in severe DENV infection.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AnxA1 is reduced in severe dengue and that disruption of the pathway worsens inflammation.

claim: Pathogenic immune responses underlie the severity of several viral diseases, including severe community-acquired pneumonia caused by viruses and COVID-19.
source: Since pathogenic immune responses are not exclusive to dengue but underlie the severity of several other viral diseases, including severe community-acquired pneumonia caused by viruses (D'Elia et al., 2013; Perrone et al., 2008) and COVID-19 (Jose and Manuel, 2020), our findings could be translated into different infectious settings, whereby targeting the AnxA1 pathway, with or without combination with antiviral drugs, holds promising therapeutic potential.
evidence: Supported by citations to publications on viral diseases and established knowledge.

claim: Targeting the AnxA1 pathway, with or without combination with antiviral drugs, holds promising therapeutic potential in viral diseases characterized by pathogenic immune responses.
source: Since pathogenic immune responses are not exclusive to dengue but underlie the severity of several other viral diseases, including severe community-acquired pneumonia caused by viruses (D'Elia et al., 2013; Perrone et al., 2008) and COVID-19 (Jose and Manuel, 2020), our findings could be translated into different infectious settings, whereby targeting the AnxA1 pathway, with or without combination with antiviral drugs, holds promising therapeutic potential.
evidence: Speculated based on the findings in dengue and the known role of pathogenic immune responses in other viral diseases.
